claims.text: Introducing a minor zirconium addition into a base alloy will enhance its glass-forming ability.
Conventional Al- or Cu-based alloys may have modest glass-forming ability.
The proposed base alloy typically crystallizes under rapid-cooling conditions.
A zirconium addition in the range of 1–5 at.% is a relevant range for improving glass-forming ability.
Adding zirconium increases atomic-size mismatch in the alloy.
Adding zirconium introduces local packing disorder.
Zirconium has a relatively large atomic radius compared with many common glass-forming elements.
Zirconium addition reduces the number of favorable nucleation sites.
The zirconium-induced structural changes retard crystallization kinetics.
Retarded crystallization kinetics stabilize the amorphous structure.
The zirconium-modified alloy will have a lower crystallization onset temperature than the baseline alloy.
The zirconium-modified alloy will have a broader supercooled-liquid region than the baseline alloy.
The zirconium-modified alloy will produce XRD patterns indicative of an amorphous structure.
Glass-forming ability can be assessed using crystallization onset temperature and amorphous phase fraction under matched cooling conditions.
The proposed effect is expected in systems whose base composition is amenable to glass formation and in which zirconium provides significant atomic-size disparity.
Competing crystallization mechanisms may alter the effect of zirconium addition.
The optimal zirconium content and magnitude of improvement may vary with base-alloy composition and cooling rate.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says zirconium retards crystallization kinetics, but the predicted outcome and falsification rule treat a lower crystallization onset temperature as an improvement. Under otherwise identical DSC conditions, a lower onset generally indicates crystallization beginning earlier, so this direction is inconsistent with the stated retardation mechanism unless an additional quantity or rationale is supplied.
